episodes.title: Flight of Booker T. Washington Jr. from Alabama
episodes.lead: The flight of Booker T. Washington Jr. from Alabama was his reported departure from the state in late 1918, after Black newspapers said he had denounced a mob that lynched a Black man at Sheffield, Alabama, named some of its members, and was then threatened with mob vengeance. No one was killed in the episode; Washington Jr., son of the founder of Tuskegee Institute, was said to have fled with his family to Ohio and then St. Louis. The story ran in at least ten Black weeklies in January 1919, though a Chattanooga minister denied that anyone had run him out of the state.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bragg Williams
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bragg Williams took place at Hillsboro, Texas, on January 20, 1919, when a mob took Williams, a Black man under sentence of death, from the Hill County jail and burned him on the public square. He had been convicted of murdering Mrs. George Wells and her child near Itasca, and the mob formed after his attorneys gave notice of appeal. Because he had already been sentenced, Black editors cited the burning against the claim that lynching answered the failure of the courts.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Marion, Ohio
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Marion, Ohio, took place in early February 1919, when a crowd stoned Black homes and warning placards ordered Black workers to leave the city after the murder of a white woman and an assault on another woman. An exodus of Black residents followed, and a man accused in the assault was moved out of the county jail after threats of lynching. A month later about thirty Black property-owning families were reported still living in the city.

episodes.title: Killing of a Black man on the Arch Street Pike, Little Rock
episodes.lead: The killing of a Black man on the Arch Street Pike was a homicide near Little Rock, Arkansas, in early 1919, in which an unnamed "Colored man" was killed and three white men were charged with murder. The Cleveland Advocate reported the case on its front page as the arrest of a white man for the death of a "Race Man."

episodes.title: Lynching of John Daniels
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Daniels took place in February 1919, when a mob took Daniels, a Black man charged with murder, from the jail at Jacksonville, North Carolina, in Onslow County, and hanged him from the Neuse River bridge. A second prisoner, Daniel Pettaway, was taken with him and was supposed to have been lynched as well. Black newspapers in Cleveland and Wisconsin reported it as another North Carolina lynching, and the Wisconsin Weekly Blade later reprinted a Raleigh editorial deploring it.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching on a Norfolk trolley car
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching on a Norfolk trolley car was an attack in Norfolk, Virginia, on the night of February 9, 1919, in which enlisted navy men seized an unidentified Black man and tried to electrocute him on a streetcar's trolley wire. A petty officer stopped them and persuaded them to leave the matter to the police. Three Black newspapers carried the story, one headlining it an attempted lynching.

episodes.title: Ku Klux Klan notices in Pittsburgh
episodes.lead: The Ku Klux Klan notices in Pittsburgh were printed threats, signed by a self-styled "Klu Klux Klan," that were posted on Black churches and homes in the East Liberty and East End districts of Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, in February 1919, warning Black residents to "stay in their place." Black newspapers from Baltimore to Phoenix carried the story, some presenting it as Klan activity spreading to the North and others printing a denial from R. R. Vann, editor of the Courier, who called the notices "evidently the work of ignorant bums." No violence, arrests or identification of the authors appear in the coverage.

episodes.title: Shooting of Ross Moore
episodes.lead: The shooting of Ross Moore was a robbery and shooting of a Black taxi driver by three young white men on the outskirts of Birmingham, Alabama, in the early morning of February 26, 1919. Moore was shot in the head and left in his car, and when the only known report was filed it was not known whether he would survive.

episodes.title: Birmingham police shooting of Albert Brown
episodes.lead: The Birmingham police shooting of Albert Brown was a gunfight in Birmingham, Alabama, in March 1919, in which two policemen fired on two Black soldiers and Brown, one of the soldiers, shot both officers before he was killed. Policemen W. D. Evans and A. W. Phillips died of their wounds a few hours later, and the other soldier escaped. Black newspapers carried it as a case of officers firing on soldiers 'without cause'.

episodes.title: Threatened Klan attack on Black residents of Birmingham (1919)
episodes.lead: The threatened Klan attack on Black residents of Birmingham was a planned massacre and expulsion of the Black population of Birmingham, Alabama, that the writer William Pickens said was set for a Saturday night in March 1919. According to Pickens, the attack was called off because Black residents were armed and ready to defend themselves, and no one was reported hurt. The Plaindealer printed his account under the headline "ARMED BLACKS AVERT HORRIBLE MASSACRE" as an example of courage averting a second East St. Louis.

episodes.title: Sardis soldier shooting
episodes.lead: The Sardis soldier shooting was a fight at Sardis, Mississippi, in late February or early March 1919, in which a Black soldier recently returned from a training camp shot two white men, Bob Bedford and Barney Nance, after white men interfered in a fight between a white boy and a Black boy. Both men died of their wounds at the Baptist Memorial Hospital in Memphis, and the soldier had not been caught when the reports ran. Black newspapers in several cities reprinted the item as a sign that returned Black soldiers would no longer accept prewar treatment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bud Johnson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Bud Johnson was the burning to death of a Black man by a mob in western Florida in March 1919, after he was taken from a sheriff's party at Castleberry while being moved away from the Pensacola jail. Johnson had been accused of attacking a white woman at Pace, Florida, and was burned near the scene of the alleged crime. The case drew wide attention in the Black press after the NAACP published Governor Sidney J. Catts's reply to its protest, in which he wrote that the lynchers could not be brought to trial in Florida.

episodes.title: Clubbing of a Black soldier by Chattanooga police (1919)
episodes.lead: The clubbing of a Black soldier by Chattanooga police took place on the evening of Monday, March 3, 1919, when Policeman J. H. Cornett struck one of a group of "Colored soldiers" on East Ninth street in Chattanooga, Tennessee. After a hearing at which many Black witnesses testified against the officers, Commissioner Betterton suspended Cornett and Patrolman Green and then discharged Cornett, who appealed to the full board. The Cleveland Advocate carried the case as news that a policeman had been dismissed for using force on a Black soldier.

episodes.title: Bombing of a flat building on Indiana Avenue, Chicago
episodes.lead: The bombing of a flat building on Indiana Avenue was an explosion in early 1919 that wrecked a three-story brick building at 3365-3401 Indiana Avenue on the South Side of Chicago, a building tenanted by Black families in an otherwise white block. Six-year-old Ernestine Ellis was killed and several members of the households living there were injured. First reports left the cause open between a dynamite bomb and defective gas pipes, but Black papers later counted it among a series of bombings of Black homes, and it figured in a June protest to Mayor William Hale Thompson.

episodes.title: Bombing of Jesse Binga's office and the Robinson residence, Chicago (March 1919)
episodes.lead: The bombing of Jesse Binga's office and the Robinson residence was a pair of bomb attacks on Black-occupied property on the South Side of Chicago, Illinois, on a single night in March 1919, apparently Wednesday, March 19. Bombs thrown from a passing automobile wrecked the real estate and banking office of Jesse Binga, a Black banker, and damaged the Calumet avenue building where the family of Alex J. Robinson lived. No one was killed, and the Black press presented the attack as the latest in a series of bombings aimed at Black families moving into formerly white sections.

episodes.title: Whipping of Clarence Cooper
episodes.lead: The whipping of Clarence Cooper was an attack on a Black landowner by a group of white men outside his church in Homer, Louisiana, on a Sunday in early March 1919. Cooper had sold his land and announced that he was moving North, and his attackers whipped him into insensibility and then told the congregation it was a warning to anyone else who left. The only known report, in the Phoenix Tribune, said the United States Department of Justice was being asked to investigate.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black workers from Coatesville, Pennsylvania
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black workers from Coatesville, Pennsylvania, was a series of police roundups in early 1919 in which a constable, local police and the state constabulary drove unemployed Black steel workers out of the town. The NAACP protested to federal and state officials, and the Department of Labor ordered an investigation. Black newspapers presented it as the treatment of war workers whose labor was no longer needed.

episodes.title: Lynching of Eugene Greene
episodes.lead: The lynching of Eugene Greene was the seizure and reported hanging of a young Black man taken by a band of men from the jail at Belzoni, Mississippi, early on Sunday, March 2, 1919, while he was held on a charge of shooting the town marshal. The Jackson Daily News, mocking an inquiry from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, wrote that he had been hanged and his body thrown into the Yazoo River, and the county sheriff was later tried for contempt over his loss.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Buckville, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Buckville, Arkansas, was a 1919 night-rider campaign in which a white band dynamited, burned and shot up the homes of a Black farming settlement about 20 miles northwest of Hot Springs. The main raid, dated to March 29, reportedly left only a Baptist minister's home standing, and the local prosecutor was quoted as saying every Black family had been driven out. In June grand jury indictments led to the arrest of six white men, two sets of brothers, on arson charges. Black newspapers presented the attack as a land grab by prominent whites and linked the accused to a newly organized Ku Klux Klan.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Gilbreath
episodes.lead: The killing of Henry Gilbreath was the fatal shooting of a Black private of the 366th Infantry by Patrolman Crump in Chattanooga, Tennessee, early on a Thursday morning in late March 1919. Crump said he fired as the soldier came at him with a knife, and a coroner's jury and an army board of officers arranged a joint inquiry into the death.

episodes.title: Threats against Henry Johnson in St. Louis
episodes.lead: The threats against Henry Johnson in St. Louis took place on March 29, 1919, when a group of Marines confronted Sergeant Henry Johnson, a decorated Black soldier from Albany, New York, at his hotel and demanded that he retract remarks made in a speech the night before. After further threats by telephone, Johnson left the city that night in disguise, while returned white soldiers obtained a federal warrant against him.

episodes.title: Killing of Warren Edwards and Henry Landers
episodes.lead: The killing of Warren Edwards and Henry Landers was the death of two Black men at the hands of a white officer in Atlanta, Georgia, reported in March 1919. According to a brief Black-press dispatch, the two had been playing cards and were killed when they tried to escape, and the dispatch called the deaths murder.

episodes.title: Threat to burn the Allen home in Hope, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The threat to burn the Allen home in Hope, Arkansas, was a warning delivered in early March 1919 by crowds of white residents to the family of Mrs. Jennie Allen, a Black woman whose French sister-in-law had come to stay with them. The visitor moved to a hotel on the advice of a local official, and no violence was reported. Several Black newspapers carried the story as an example of how Black soldiers and their French wives were treated on their return from the war.

episodes.title: Attempted removal of a wounded Black soldier from a Texas sleeping car
episodes.lead: The attempted removal of a wounded Black soldier from a Texas sleeping car was an incident in early 1919 in which white passengers objected to a Black veteran riding in a sleeper on a federally operated train. The objectors stood aside after the soldier's white lieutenant said he would be removed only over the officer's dead body. The Dallas Express used the incident in an editorial against Jim Crow and "white supremacy."

episodes.title: Beal Street automobile shooting (1919)
episodes.lead: The Beal Street automobile shooting was an attack in Memphis, Tennessee, in March 1919, in which two white men firing from an automobile killed James Anderson, a Black man, and wounded three other Black men as they came out of a cafe on Beal street. The men escaped, and police had not identified them when the only known report was published.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joe Walker
episodes.lead: The lynching of Joe Walker was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Greenville, Florida, in March 1919, after he was taken from two police officers who were carrying him to jail at Madison. Walker had been charged with shooting a night watchman, and he was shot to death without trial. The case reached Black readers through a brief Valdosta, Georgia, dispatch and through the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People's protest to Governor Sidney J. Catts, whose reply that lynchers could not be brought to trial was printed across the Black press.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Pauline Willis from Yazoo City
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Pauline Willis from Yazoo City was the forcing out of a young Black woman from Yazoo City, Mississippi, in early 1919 because she sold Black newspapers there. No violence was reported, but Black weeklies from St. Louis to Milwaukee carried the story as an example of white efforts to keep the race press out of the South.

episodes.title: Ordered whipping of Rev. Thomas Collins
episodes.lead: The ordered whipping of Rev. Thomas Collins took place in Yazoo, Mississippi, in about March 1919, when the town's white Commercial Club ordered the Black minister and four other colored citizens beaten for defying a ban on Black newspapers. Collins escaped on the way to the whipping post and fled to Philadelphia, and the Baltimore Afro-American presented his case as an example of a "Ku Klux Law Against Reading Colored Newspapers and Magazines."

episodes.title: Expulsion of Bob Williamson from Cordale, Georgia
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Bob Williamson from Cordale, Georgia, was an attack on a traveling picture salesman by white people who objected to his selling photographs of Sergeant Henry Johnson, reported in a dispatch dated April 4, 1919. Williamson's pictures were torn up, a pistol was put in his mouth, and he was ordered to leave town, which he did. The Chicago Defender carried the story on its front page as an example of Southern hostility to images of Black soldiers' war service.

episodes.title: Ellis Avenue bombing
episodes.lead: The Ellis Avenue bombing was the explosion of a bomb at the property of J. C. Yarbrough, 3212-14 Ellis avenue, Chicago, at 2 a.m. on a Monday in April 1919, set off by unknown parties. No one was reported hurt, but the blast wrecked furniture in two flats and, according to the Chicago Defender, endangered the lives of six families. The Defender reported it as further evidence that "bomb throwers" were operating "unmolested" in the city.

episodes.title: 1919 Millen race riot
episodes.lead: The 1919 Millen race riot was an outbreak of violence near Millen, Georgia, on April 13, 1919, that began when two white officers arrested a Black man at a church gathering and left both officers and at least four Black men dead. Afterward a white mob burned Black churches, lodge halls and automobiles, and Black papers reported at least one further Black man lynched. Black editors treated the episode as an attack on prosperous Black farmers.

episodes.title: Pine Street attack on George Graham's home (Philadelphia, 1919)
episodes.lead: The Pine Street attack on George Graham's home was an assault by a crowd of white men on the house of a newly arrived Black tenant near 25th and Pine streets in Philadelphia in late April 1919. Black residents met the attackers with gunfire, and between three and nine white men were wounded before police ended the fight. Black newspapers across the country reported it as a white attack on a Black home that the residents had beaten back.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Holden
episodes.lead: The lynching of George Holden (George Bolden in the New York Age) was the shooting of a Black man by an armed mob that stopped a train west of Monroe, Louisiana, in late April 1919. Accused of writing an insulting note to a white woman, he was killed the day after nurses at a Monroe hospital turned back a masked mob that had come for him. The NAACP cited the case to Louisiana's governor before its National Conference on Lynching, and Black papers reprinted white Louisiana condemnation of the raid.

episodes.title: Beating of Henry Proctor
episodes.lead: The beating of Henry Proctor was an attack on a 16-year-old Black high-school student by six white boys armed with sticks at Forty-third Street and Forrestville Avenue on the South Side of Chicago, Illinois, around the end of April 1919. The Chicago Broad Ax reported it as "further evidence of racial bitterness on the south side" under a headline presenting it as part of a continuing "race war."

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Isaiah Fountain
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Isaiah Fountain took place at Easton, Talbot County, Maryland, in April 1919, when crowds of white farmers tried to seize a Black farmer from Trappe who was on trial for an alleged criminal assault on a white girl. Fountain escaped during a rush on his police escort, was recaptured in Delaware, and was convicted and sentenced to death; his lawyer appealed on the ground that the mob had made a fair trial impossible. The Baltimore Afro-American, which sent its own correspondents, covered the case for three months and treated the trial as nearly a lynching.

episodes.title: Kansas City housing dynamitings of 1919
episodes.lead: The Kansas City housing dynamitings of 1919 were a series of threats and dynamite attacks in the spring of 1919 against Black residents who had bought homes in white districts of Kansas City, Missouri. Black papers reported that several Black homes were damaged by "unknown enemies," and that on a Tuesday night in mid-May a charge of dynamite damaged New Hope Baptist Church at 19th and Waldron. No one was reported hurt, and the attacks came while a committee appointed by Mayor Cowgill was meeting Black leaders over the dispute.

episodes.title: Lynching of Wilbur Little
episodes.lead: The lynching of Wilbur Little was the killing of a Black returned soldier, named in the Black press as Private Wilbur Little or Private Wylie Jr. Little, who was beaten to death by a mob near Blakely, Georgia, shortly before April 4, 1919. According to the only news dispatch on the case, he had been ordered to stop wearing his army uniform and told to leave town, and he was attacked after he refused. Black papers held the case up as an example of the treatment Black soldiers met in the South on their return from the war.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Robert Porterfield
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Robert Porterfield took place in Montgomery, Alabama, in April 1919, after Porterfield, a Black man, shot police officer J. Earl Davis in a gunfight that began with Davis's arrest of Porterfield's wife. When a correspondent overheard white men discussing a possible lynching of the prisoner, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People appealed to Governor Thomas E. Kilby, who had Porterfield removed to Mobile for safe keeping. The NAACP publicized the governor's reply as a contrast to Mississippi governor Theodore G. Bilbo's response to the Shubuta lynchings.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam McIntyre
episodes.lead: The lynching of Sam McIntyre was the killing of a Black man held on a murder charge, who was taken from the county jail at Forrest City, Arkansas, by a masked mob and hanged to a telegraph pole on or about April 23, 1919. The reports said the mob acted out of anger that his lawyers had won a postponement of his trial. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People protested to Governor Charles H. Brough, calling it the twenty-first known lynching since the armistice, and its telegram made the case a news item across the Black press.

episodes.title: Lynching of Benjamin Richards
episodes.lead: The lynching of Benjamin Richards was the shooting and burning of a Black farmer by a posse and crowd at Warrenton, Georgia, early on May 2, 1919, after a night-long manhunt in a nearby swamp. Richards, accused of killing his wife, had wounded four white men, among them the sheriff, before he was shot and his body burned before about 300 people. The NAACP cited the case in a telegram to Governor Hugh M. Dorsey on the eve of the National Conference on Lynching.

episodes.title: Beating of Daniel Mack
episodes.lead: The beating of Daniel Mack was the removal of a recently discharged Black soldier from the town lockup at Sylvester, Worth County, Georgia, by armed white men, who beat him severely, on a Monday night in spring 1919 shortly before May 3. The fullest report said Mack survived with a fractured skull and was hidden by his relatives, while other Black papers reported him beaten to death or 'believed lynched.' Black weeklies treated the attack as a case of a returned soldier abused in the South.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black leaders from Bogalusa, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black leaders from Bogalusa, Louisiana, took place in spring 1919, when a committee of white citizens ordered several Black physicians, ministers and property owners to leave town before sunrise. The men left, and the Chicago Defender presented the order as a scheme to take their real estate.

episodes.title: Huntsville mob beatings of May 1919
episodes.lead: The Huntsville mob beatings of May 1919 were assaults on five Black men by a mob near Huntsville, Walker County, Texas, on May 26, 1919, during a search for a Black man a white schoolgirl said she had seen behind an abandoned house. The girl said none of the men brought before her was the one she saw, but the mob beat all of them, left Ed Morgan unconscious, and threatened to kill his family. The Houston Informer gave the attack a front-page banner; the Baltimore Afro-American condensed it a week later.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Livingston
episodes.lead: The lynching of Frank Livingston was the killing of a Black farm hand and recently discharged soldier who was tied to a tree and burned to death by a mob near Eldorado, Union County, Arkansas, on May 21, 1919. He had been accused of killing his white employer and the employer's wife after a quarrel. No arrests were reported, and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People protested to Governor Charles Brough, calling it the second lynching in Arkansas within thirty days.

episodes.title: Charleston riot of May 1919
episodes.lead: The Charleston riot of May 1919 was an attack on Black residents of Charleston, South Carolina, by sailors from the city's navy yard and training camp, joined by some white civilians, on the night of May 10, 1919. Two Black men, James Talbot and Isaac Doctor, were reported killed, and thirteen to seventeen Black people and several sailors were wounded. Black newspapers likened it to the 1917 Houston riot and stressed that only Black people were attacked.

episodes.title: Lynching of James Waters
episodes.lead: The lynching of James Waters was the killing of a Black farmhand by a mob of about 150 men in Johnson County, Georgia, in mid-May 1919, after he was accused of attacking a white girl. The men took Waters from a deputy sheriff who was driving him to the Macon jail, tied him to a tree and shot him, and a coroner's inquest attributed his death to unknown persons. The Chicago Defender reported a different account in which Waters denied the charge, which it linked to his plan to leave his employer's farm.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Biyard
episodes.lead: The killing of Joe Biyard was the fatal police shooting of a dock worker on Fahm street, near Bay, on the morning of May 2, 1919, reported by the Savannah Tribune. Biyard was shot after he objected to an officer's treatment of a woman under arrest, and according to the paper a second officer then shot him three times inside a store.

episodes.title: Police beating of Leon Hunt
episodes.lead: The police beating of Leon Hunt occurred in Baltimore's Northwestern police section shortly before May 2, 1919, when officers answering a street fight reportedly shot a man in the leg and clubbed Hunt and Percy Stimenee. The Baltimore Afro-American presented it as an example of police beating Black residents for minor offenses.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lloyd Clay
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lloyd Clay took place in Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the night of May 14, 1919, when a mob of 800 to 1,000 took Clay, a young Black man, from the county jail, hanged and burned him and shot into his body. He was accused of attempted criminal assault on a young white woman who did not identify him. Black papers presented it as the burning of an innocent man, and the NAACP pressed Mississippi's governor to try the lynchers.

episodes.title: Lynching near Mineral Wells, Mississippi (1919)
episodes.lead: The lynching near Mineral Wells, Mississippi, was the killing of an unnamed Black man, reported on 28 May 1919, after he was accused of attempting to attack a white woman on a country road. An alleged accomplice was arrested by the sheriff and moved for safekeeping, and the case is known only from a brief Memphis dispatch that the Richmond Planet printed under the headline "Another Lynching."

episodes.title: Bombing of the Gertrude Harrison residence
episodes.lead: The bombing of the Gertrude Harrison residence was a pair of bomb attacks in May 1919 on the home of Mrs. Gertrude Harrison, a Black resident of 4807 Grand boulevard in Chicago, Illinois. The second bomb, around May 29, damaged only a skylight and two back windows, and no arrest was reported. The Black press carried the story as part of a run of bombings of Black homes in the city, and the Chicago Defender blamed the police for a perfunctory investigation.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Paul Bates
episodes.lead: The threatened lynching of Paul Bates took place in Screven County, Georgia, where Bates, a Black tenant charged with killing Grady Oliver, nearly was lynched in jail before troops were called out against a mob. Bates was then tried under military guard and hanged in May 1919; the Savannah Tribune argued that no fair trial was possible under a mob's threat.

episodes.title: Lynching of a discharged soldier and a woman near Pickens, Mississippi
episodes.lead: The lynching of a discharged soldier and a woman near Pickens, Mississippi, was the reported killing of two unnamed Black people on the outskirts of Pickens, Holmes County, on or shortly before May 12, 1919. According to a dispatch from Durant, the lynching followed the man's reported admission that he had hired the woman to write an "improper note" to a young woman at Pickens. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People later cited the case in a telegram pressing Governor Theodore G. Bilbo over Mississippi's run of lynchings.

episodes.title: Hazing of the Cortney brothers at the University of Maine
episodes.lead: The hazing of the Cortney brothers was an attack in late April or early May 1919 in which white students at the University of Maine in Orono covered two Black sophomores, Roger and Daniel (or Samuel) Cortney, with molasses and feathers. Black newspapers reported it as the tarring and feathering of 'Negro students' by a mob, while the university's president issued a statement denying that race was the cause.

episodes.title: Bombing of New Hope Baptist Church, Kansas City
episodes.lead: The bombing of New Hope Baptist Church was a dynamite attack on a Black Baptist church at 19th Street and Waldron Avenue on the East Side of Kansas City, Missouri, on a Tuesday night in mid-May 1919, apparently May 13. The explosion damaged the church and nearby homes but injured no one reported, and no one was identified as the bomber. The Kansas City Sun called it "A DASTARDLY OUTRAGE" and tied it to threats against Black property, and its account was reprinted in the Metropolis Weekly Gazette and the Tulsa Star.

episodes.title: South Side Chicago boys' riot of April 1919
episodes.lead: The South Side Chicago boys' riot of April 1919 was a fight between white and Black boys, taken up by their parents, in a South Side neighborhood of Chicago, Illinois, during the last week of April 1919, in which William Epps, a 23-year-old Black man, was shot. Police reserves ended the fighting, and Epps was reported to be at the point of death in Provident Hospital. The Associated Negro Press disputed the Chicago dailies' account of how it began, and Black weeklies across the country printed its version.

episodes.title: Exclusion of William Floyd from his Oklahoma City home
episodes.lead: The exclusion of William Floyd from his Oklahoma City home was a 1919 episode in which police, enforcing a segregation ordinance, arrested a Black man for moving into a house he had bought on a white-majority block and kept him out of it under armed guard. After a month of court hearings, the charge was dismissed in mid-June and Floyd moved in despite a published statement that the house would be dynamited. The Black Dispatch followed the case weekly, publicizing a city attorney's courtroom remark about "DEAD NIGGERS" and hailing the dismissal as "a decisive victory for Black Manhood."

episodes.title: Lynching of William Moore
episodes.lead: The lynching of William Moore was the killing of a Black man by a mob in southern Mississippi on May 20, 1919, after he was accused of shooting the manager of a sawmill or lumber camp. Black newspapers placed the lynching at McHenry or near Ten Mile and reported that Moore was taken from a train and hanged from a tree. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) cited the case in a telegram to Governor Theodore G. Bilbo, counting it as the fifth lynching in Mississippi in less than three months.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Woodson Towns
episodes.lead: The attempted lynching of Woodson Towns was a mob's effort in Memphis, Tennessee, in the spring of 1919 to seize Towns, a Black street car passenger who had been wounded after a conductor was shot. Sheriff Oliver Hazard Perry turned the mob away at the county jail, and the Chicago Defender reported that there was neither a riot nor a lynching.

episodes.title: Police clubbing of a 15th Infantry soldier at a Lenox Avenue tailor shop
episodes.lead: The police clubbing of a 15th Infantry soldier at a Lenox Avenue tailor shop took place in Harlem, New York City, on or about June 20, 1919, when Officer Collins of the 38th precinct beat a soldier over the head and arrested him for assault. A crowd of about 1,000 gathered in protest, and the Chicago Defender reported the episode on its front page under a headline saying citizens had been aroused by the policeman's conduct.

episodes.title: June 1919 Prairie Avenue bombings
episodes.lead: The June 1919 Prairie Avenue bombings were dynamite explosions at buildings occupied by Black tenants on Prairie Avenue and nearby streets on the South Side of Chicago, followed by the arrest of a man found with a bomb. No one was reported hurt, and the damage fell on building entrances. Chicago's Black weeklies treated the arrest as a rare break in a run of bombings of Black homes, and the Chicago Whip used it to accuse a white property owners' association of directing the attacks.

episodes.title: Cincinnati near-riot of 1919
episodes.lead: The Cincinnati near-riot of 1919 was a street fight in Cincinnati, Ohio, that began when white men struck a Black child and Black men returned to the scene. Police arrived in force and ended the fight, and the Cleveland Advocate reported the episode in June 1919 as a race riot "narrowly averted."

episodes.title: Lynching of Clyde Ellison
episodes.lead: The lynching of Clyde Ellison was the hanging of a Black man by a mob from a bridge about three miles from Star City, Arkansas, on a Friday morning in mid-June 1919. A Star City report blamed an alleged attempt to attack a young woman, but a Century News Service dispatch said Ellison was killed for refusing to work for a white farmer for 85 cents a day and that the assault charge was a plot. Black papers reported that he was tortured with heated flat irons and left hanging overnight under a warning sign, and the Colorado Statesman named the killing in an editorial on recent outrages.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Dudley Singleton
episodes.lead: The police shooting of Dudley Singleton took place shortly after noon on Monday, 23 June 1919, when Patrolman Walker of Cleveland's E. 37th St. station shot Singleton, a Black man, in the left leg and abdomen during a fight in a Central Avenue poolroom. The Cleveland Gazette described the wounding as probably fatal, and a week later Singleton's name appeared on an undertakers' list in the Cleveland Advocate.

episodes.title: 1919 Vernon Avenue boys' fight, Chicago
episodes.lead: The 1919 Vernon Avenue boys' fight was a clash on Chicago's South Side on a Monday afternoon in early June 1919, in which white boys and white spectators attacked Black boys with bricks and stones. No one was reported killed or hurt, but police arriving on a riot call took several Black boys away in a patrol wagon. The Chicago Defender reported it as a "miniature Race riot" and contrasted its own boys with whites "of the ruffian type."

episodes.title: Rumored Ferguson raid on Lix Park, Kinloch
episodes.lead: The rumored Ferguson raid on Lix Park was a June 1919 scare in Kinloch, St. Louis County, Missouri, when residents expected people from neighboring Ferguson to raid the Lix Park outing place at night. Many Kinloch women and children left for the night, but no mob came. The St. Louis Argus reported the episode to correct what it called an exaggerated account in a St. Louis daily.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Jackson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Charles Jackson was the killing of Charles W. Jackson, a Black man, by a mob of white men at 13th and Robey streets in Chicago on a Monday night, apparently June 30, 1919. His brother James Jackson was beaten by the mob and then arrested by police, and five members of the mob were reported shot. The Chicago Defender called the killing a lynching and dismissed the mob's claim that the brothers had insulted two Jewish girls as a pretext.

episodes.title: Macon, Mississippi floggings of 1919
episodes.lead: The Macon, Mississippi floggings of 1919 were an attack on Saturday night, June 7, 1919, in which white men flogged several leading Black citizens of Macon and white residents then robbed Black homes and stores. No arrests had been reported by mid-June. The New York Age editorialized on the case because, by its account, a banker, a deputy sheriff and the city marshal led the floggings.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim McMillan
episodes.lead: The lynching of Jim McMillan was the killing of a Black man by a mob of white men near Green Pond, Alabama, in mid-June 1919, during a search for a man accused of an attempted assault on a white woman. The same mob drove George Lightsey, a Black landowner, from his home, and four white men were jailed on a charge of being members of the party that shot McMillan.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Hartfield
episodes.lead: The lynching of John Hartfield took place on June 26, 1919, near Ellisville, Mississippi, where a crowd hanged Hartfield, a Black man accused of assaulting a young white woman, and burned his body. He had been badly wounded at his capture, and the Black press covered the case widely, largely because Governor Theodore G. Bilbo had said beforehand that he was "utterly powerless" to stop it.

episodes.title: Beating of Lieutenant Marion R. Perry
episodes.lead: The beating of Lieutenant Marion R. Perry took place at Peffler's department store in Little Rock, Arkansas, on or shortly before June 20, 1919, when store clerks attacked the army officer after he protested being refused a money order. Perry was left bleeding from several wounds, and the clerk who struck first was arrested. Black newspapers presented the case as an insult to a returned soldier, and one counted it among the outrages of that year.

episodes.title: Police beating of a Black woman at Ninth and Santa Fe Avenue, Los Angeles
episodes.lead: The police beating of a Black woman at Ninth and Santa Fe Avenue was an assault by two officers, Winget and Fritol, on an unnamed "Colored woman" they had arrested, at that corner in Los Angeles on a Friday evening in late June or early July 1919. When a witness, H. A. Reeves, asked about the beating, the officers arrested him. The California Eagle reported the episode as an instance of habitual police mistreatment and announced that local organizations would bring a case against the officers.

episodes.title: Arrest of Mabel Puffer and Arthur Hazzard
episodes.lead: The arrest of Mabel Puffer and Arthur Hazzard took place in Concord, New Hampshire, in June 1919, when Massachusetts officials arrested Mabel Emeline Puffer, a white woman of Ayer, Massachusetts, and her fiancé Arthur Garfield Hazzard, a Black man, shortly before their planned wedding and took both to Boston. Hazzard was held on a statutory charge later described as enticement, and Puffer on an insanity warrant sworn out by a niece. By July 11 the charges against Hazzard had been dropped and a court had declared Puffer insane, an outcome the Chicago Defender headlined "Prejudice Wins Out in Intermarriage Case."

episodes.title: Ku Klux Klan demonstration in Montgomery (1919)
episodes.lead: The Ku Klux Klan demonstration in Montgomery was a night visit to Montgomery, Alabama, by a group calling itself the Ku Klux Klan, reported by a Montgomery daily paper in 1919. No violence or victim was reported, but the account reached the Black press in June 1919 as evidence of a revived Klan meant to intimidate returning Black soldiers.

episodes.title: Whipping of Moses M. Dempster
episodes.lead: The whipping of Moses M. Dempster was a mob beating of a Black man near Monticello, Mississippi, reported under a June 1, 1919, dateline. Accused of shooting at a bill collector, Dempster was taken into the woods by armed men and beaten with a buggy trace, and the report credited a sheriff's plea for "the whip instead of the rope" with saving his life.

episodes.title: Stoning of the Sheppard home, Chicago
episodes.lead: The stoning of the Sheppard home was an attack in June 1919 by about fifty white men and boys on the newly bought bungalow of Mr. and Mrs. B. F. Sheppard at 6718 Calumet avenue in Chicago, Illinois. The crowd broke every window in the house, and a second stoning followed about ten days later, when shots were fired at the attackers. Chicago's Black weeklies covered it as an attack the police had failed to stop and as a case of a family that refused to be driven out.

episodes.title: New London sailors' riot
episodes.lead: The New London sailors' riot was a series of clashes between Black and white sailors in New London, Connecticut, in early June 1919 that ended in a raid by white sailors on a hotel for Black guests and a street battle on Bank Street. Town police and firemen could not stop the fighting, and a detachment of United States Marines restored order. The Black press carried the story through an Associated Negro Press dispatch, which the St. Louis Argus headlined as a riot "Started By Whites."

episodes.title: Omaha teamsters' strike circular (1919)
episodes.lead: The Omaha teamsters' strike circular was a printed warning issued in June 1919 by Teamsters' Union Local 211 in Omaha, Nebraska, during a strike, claiming that Black strikebreakers were being brought from East St. Louis. The circular urged residents to protect their families and homes and called on a local revolver club to "take notice". The Monitor, Omaha's Black weekly, reprinted it, called the report of strikebreakers false, and accused the union of stirring up prejudice against the race.

episodes.title: Putnam County church burnings
episodes.lead: The Putnam County church burnings were the burning of five Black churches, two schools and a lodge hall near Dennis Station, outside Eatonton in Putnam County, Georgia, in the spring of 1919, attributed to a party of white men said to have revived the Ku Klux Klan. No one was reported killed in the fires, and no report of an arrest appears in the coverage. Black weeklies across the country carried the story under headlines naming the Klan, and Black editorials cited it among the year's outrages against Black Americans.

episodes.title: Columbian Union Klan circular in Richmond, Virginia
episodes.lead: The Columbian Union Klan circular in Richmond, Virginia, was a 1919 letter calling white citizens to a masked meeting at the Business Men's Club to organize a 'new Richmond Klan' as a successor to the Ku Klux Klan of Reconstruction. The Richmond Planet published the letter on July 5, 1919, and read it as an effort to tell Black people to stay away from the city. No violence was reported, but the publication drew protest from Black ministers and returned soldiers in Richmond.

episodes.title: Lynching of Robert Robinson
episodes.lead: The lynching of Robert Robinson was the killing of Robinson, a Black man living at 514 West 54th Place on Chicago's South Side, by a mob of white men around midnight on Saturday, June 21, 1919. The same mob shot and stabbed Ollie Harris, who was reported dying, and part of it was said to have beaten a former soldier, Charles Mitchell. Black papers in several states reported the attack as a "race war" started by whites.

episodes.title: St. Louis Workhouse quarry bombing
episodes.lead: The St. Louis Workhouse quarry bombing was an explosion on June 12, 1919, in the rock quarry of the City Workhouse in St. Louis, Missouri, in which a white prisoner threw an explosive among Black prisoners, injuring eleven to thirteen of them. St. Louis daily papers reported the episode as a "race riot" in which guards fired on fighting prisoners, a version that also reached the Wisconsin Weekly Blade. The St. Louis Argus, a Black weekly, investigated and called those reports "false and misleading", describing instead one man's act followed by an attempted mass escape by white prisoners.

episodes.title: Killing of Joseph Turner
episodes.lead: The killing of Joseph Turner was the fatal shooting of a Memphis storekeeper by Deputy Sheriff Jim Reynolds at Turner's store on South Trezevant street in late June 1919. Reynolds had come with a white creditor, J. E. McCallum, to collect a debt; he was shot in the struggle and reportedly died the next day. The Chicago Defender carried the story on its front page and later reported a bystander's suit against the sheriff.

episodes.title: Vicksburg bulldog lynching
episodes.lead: The Vicksburg bulldog lynching was the killing of an unnamed Black man by a white mob in Vicksburg, Mississippi, in late June 1919, after he was accused of intimacy with a white woman. According to the Chicago Whip, the mob buried him to the neck, set a bulldog maddened with red pepper on his head inside an iron cage, and forced prominent Black residents to watch. The Whip, the only paper found with a full account, presented the killing as a crime that the white press had suppressed.

episodes.title: Shooting of Wayman Booker
episodes.lead: The shooting of Wayman Booker was an attack on a resident of Shamrock, Kentucky, by four white men on a drunken spree, reported in a dispatch dated June 13, 1919. Booker was shot four times in the abdomen and described as fatally wounded, and the men escaped with no reward offered for their capture. The Chicago Defender carried the only known report, on its front page.

episodes.title: Bombing of William Austin's home
episodes.lead: The bombing of William Austin's home was a dynamite attack in mid-June 1919 on the Lake Shore Drive residence of William Austin, a Chicago man who owned South Side property occupied by Black tenants. Black papers tied the explosion, which damaged the house, to an anonymous warning that Austin get rid of his "Colored" tenants.

episodes.title: Whipping of William Perkins
episodes.lead: The whipping of William Perkins was an attack on a Black man at Hulbert, Arkansas, reported in a dispatch dated June 27, 1919, in which a group of white men seized him, carried him to the swamps and lashed him. According to the report, he was punished for telling people how well Black people were treated in Chicago, and several other people were ordered to leave the town. The Chicago Defender carried the story on its front page under a headline calling it a murder, although its text describes a beating followed by a trip to the hospital.

episodes.title: Shooting of Ed Gardner
episodes.lead: The shooting of Ed Gardner took place in the jail at Murray, Kentucky, on Monday, July 7, 1919, when a Black prisoner was shot in the leg during an argument with jailer Albert James and his guards. Gardner, who had been held on a whiskey-selling charge, then faced a charge of assault, according to a brief dispatch printed in the Dallas Express.

episodes.title: Bisbee clash between police and Tenth Cavalry troopers (1919)
episodes.lead: The Bisbee clash between police and Tenth Cavalry troopers was a street fight in Bisbee, Arizona, on the night of July 3-4, 1919, in which city police and white civilians tried to disarm Black soldiers of the 10th U.S. Cavalry who had come to town for the Fourth of July parade. Five people were reported wounded, among them three troopers and a white deputy sheriff, and fourteen soldiers were arrested and handed over to the military authorities. Black papers in Chicago, Baltimore, Dallas and Phoenix carried the story, blaming a white military policeman's insult or the police.

episodes.title: Lynching of Lemmel Walters
episodes.lead: The lynching of Lemmel Walters was the killing of a 17-year-old Black man in Longview, Texas, who was taken from the town jail by a crowd of white men and shot on or shortly before July 4, 1919. No charge had been made against him, and the only cause the report gave was a white woman's statement that she loved him. The Chicago Defender reported the killing under a headline accusing local police of trying to keep it secret.

episodes.title: Stoning of the Barred home on Mosher Street
episodes.lead: The stoning of the Barred home on Mosher Street was an attack in July 1919 in which whites threw stones and bricks through the windows of a house newly occupied by a Black family, Mr. and Mrs. James Barred. No one was hurt, and after a crowd that included Black soldiers in uniform gathered and the whites withdrew, one white man and two Black men were arrested. The Baltimore Afro-American reported it as a reaction to Black families buying homes in the block.

episodes.title: Killing of a Black youth near Camden, Arkansas
episodes.lead: The killing of a Black youth near Camden, Arkansas, was the shooting of a colored farmer's son by a white man and two companions, who took him out of a church service and shot him before about 125 onlookers, as reported in July 1919. The New York Age cited the case as an example of "Southern manners" and called it the "murder of an unoffending youth."

episodes.title: Shooting of Price Hartgrave
episodes.lead: The shooting of Price Hartgrave took place on July 4, 1919, in Brooklyn, New York, when a police officer shot Hartgrave, 30, after a raid on a crap game. Police said he had attacked an officer with a blade; his friends said he was dragged from his home and shot while held. The Chicago Defender printed both versions, the second as part of a charge of police brutality toward Black residents of the neighborhood.

episodes.title: Pulaski camp meeting raid
episodes.lead: The Pulaski camp meeting raid was an attack by white deputy sheriffs on a large Black camp meeting at Pulaski, Georgia, reported under a July 4, 1919, dateline. The deputies beat many people about the head, several persons were shot, and with the help of white men from the community the meeting was broken up and prisoners were taken to the county seat. The Chicago Defender ran the story on its front page and compared it to an earlier deputies' action at Millen, Georgia.

episodes.title: Montgomery County Klan intimidation
episodes.lead: The Montgomery County Klan intimidation was a campaign in the weeks before July 5, 1919, in which white residents of Montgomery County, Maryland, organized a "Ku Klux Klan" and white gangs terrorized Black men during a hunt for a Black man accused of assaulting women. The Baltimore Afro-American reported that the group also meant to keep the area's Black population "in order"; no deaths or injuries were reported.

episodes.title: Killing of Nathan Green
episodes.lead: The killing of Nathan Green was the fatal shooting of a Black man, also called Charlie Williams, by a citizens' posse of about forty in the Madison section of Nashville, Tennessee, early on Friday, July 11, 1919. Green, accused of burglary, died a few hours later at the county jail, and two Black members of the posse were seriously wounded in the chase.

episodes.title: Beating of Benjamin Herne
episodes.lead: The beating of Benjamin Herne was an assault in Atlanta, Georgia, in early May 1919, in which a white drug-store clerk named Powell struck Herne, a Black soldier recently returned from France, on the head with a baseball bat after Herne asked for a drink at the store's soda fountain. Herne was carried insensible to Grady Hospital, and most reports said Powell was arrested for "disorderly conduct." The Associated Negro Press spread the story to Black papers across the country as a sign of how returned Black soldiers were treated in the South, and a Macon newspaper's defense of the beating drew a reply from the Chicago Defender.

episodes.title: Theft of a Black Pullman passenger's shoes near Cairo, Illinois
episodes.lead: The theft of a Black Pullman passenger's shoes near Cairo, Illinois, was an undated incident in which several white passengers on a train from Chicago threw a Black man's shoes out of the window overnight, leaving him to leave the train at Cairo in his socks. It is known only from a white Jackson, Mississippi, columnist's own recollection, told as a joke and reprinted by the New York Age on June 21, 1919.

episodes.title: Assault on a Black soldier at Delta, Louisiana
episodes.lead: The assault on a Black soldier at Delta, Louisiana, was an attack in which an unnamed "colored soldier" riding in a sleeping car was taken out at Delta, across the Mississippi River from Vicksburg, shortly before June 1919 and, according to Southern papers, "roughly handled." The only account is a passage in a Chicago Broad Ax editorial of June 7, 1919, which said the soldier's fate was unknown. The writer offered the case as an example of what he called a "reign of terror" against Black veterans returning from France.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Black residents from Dewey, Oklahoma
episodes.lead: The expulsion of Black residents from Dewey, Oklahoma, was an attack, reported in early 1919, in which a mob destroyed the homes of Black men and women at Dewey and drove them from the town. It is known from the Black press of Oklahoma, where Oklahoma City Black leaders cited it in an address to the Governor and the attorney W. H. Twine brought a bill to reimburse the victims.

episodes.title: Intimidation of a Black newspaper publisher near Paris, Kentucky
episodes.lead: The intimidation of a Black newspaper publisher near Paris, Kentucky, was an attack, probably in the first half of 1919, in which white-robed horsemen seized the publisher of a Black-owned paper that had urged local workers to organize. The episode is known only from a minister's report to the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People's annual conference, as relayed by the Cleveland Gazette, which said the publisher was terrorized into silence.
